chapters.situation: Gandhi's ships, the Courland and the Naderi with about 800 Indians, have anchored at Durban. A garbled Reuters summary of his Green Pamphlet has already reached Natal.
chapters.summary: Durban's whites agitate to send the ships back, and the government uses a 23-day 'plague' quarantine to intimidate the passengers. Gandhi is accused of slandering Natal in India and of bringing in shiploads of Indians to swamp the colony. At a Christmas dinner on board he calls Western civilization one based on force, and tells the captain he hopes he would forgive attackers rather than sue. Gandhi and the passengers reject the ultimatums and are finally allowed to land.

updates.gandhi: The main target of Durban's white agitation. Keeps up the passengers' spirits and says that if attacked he would forgive rather than prosecute.
updates.abdulla: His firm, managed by Abdul Karim Haji Adam, refuses bribes and threats to send the ships back.
updates.naazar: In Durban to meet Gandhi; capably leads the community during the crisis.
updates.laughton: The firm's fearless advocate; condemns the white agitators.
updates.escombe: The most influential cabinet minister; openly joins the anti-Indian meetings.
updates.kasturba: Endures the quarantine and threats aboard ship with her children.
updates.courland: Held in quarantine for 23 days as a pretext for coercion.
updates.racism: Mass white meetings demand that the Indians be turned back.
updates.ahimsa: Gandhi tells the captain he would forgive attackers, pitying their ignorance.
updates.greenpamphlet: Its exaggerated Reuters summary turns Durban's whites against Gandhi.

chapters.situation: After 23 days of quarantine and threats, the passengers are finally allowed to land at Durban, but Gandhi is the special target of the whites' anger.
chapters.summary: Laughton persuades Gandhi not to slip ashore at night. Kasturbai and the children drive to Rustomji's house while Gandhi and Laughton walk. A mob recognizes Gandhi, separates them, and stones, kicks and beats him until Mrs. Alexander, the police superintendent's wife, shields him with her parasol. That night the mob surrounds Rustomji's house, and Gandhi escapes disguised as an Indian constable while Superintendent Alexander keeps the crowd singing. Chamberlain asks Natal to prosecute, but Gandhi refuses, blaming the leaders, including Escombe, more than the mob.

updates.gandhi: Lynched by a white mob in Durban and rescued; escapes in disguise. Refuses to prosecute his attackers and gives Escombe this in writing.
updates.laughton: Advises landing openly by day and walks with Gandhi until the mob separates them.
updates.alexander: Mrs. Alexander shields Gandhi with her parasol. The Superintendent sends police, then gets Gandhi out in disguise and pacifies the crowd with humour.
updates.rustomji: Shelters Gandhi's family; his house is besieged by the mob.
updates.kasturba: Goes ahead safely to Rustomji's house with the children; the mob threatens the house that night.
updates.escombe: Expresses regret and offers prosecution. Gandhi tells him the leaders, himself included, are more to blame than the mob.
updates.chamberlain: Cables Natal to prosecute Gandhi's assailants.
updates.ahimsa: Gandhi refuses to prosecute: the mob acted on false reports, and they will be sorry once they learn the truth.
updates.racism: Gandhi is beaten by a white mob on landing at Durban.
updates.natal: Durban is the scene of the mob attack and the siege of Rustomji's house.

status.gandhi: Recovering from the mob attack, sheltered at a police station

chapters.situation: Gandhi has survived a lynching by a white mob on landing and refused to prosecute his attackers.
chapters.summary: Gandhi's interview with The Natal Advertiser, backed by his written Indian speeches, clears him. Together with his refusal to prosecute, it shames Durban's whites, and the press declares him innocent. But the Indians' show of spirit prompts two new laws, nominally colour-blind, targeting Indian traders and immigration. Congress funds grow to £5,000 and buy rental property. Gandhi later decides public institutions should live on yearly subscriptions, not permanent funds.

updates.gandhi: Cleared by the press; his practice grows. Public work now takes most of his time.
updates.pherozeshah: His insistence on written speeches lets Gandhi prove what he actually said in India.
updates.adamji: Served well as acting secretary, adding about £1,000 to Congress funds.
updates.naazar: Moves in with Gandhi and shares the public work.
updates.nic: Funds reach £5,000 and buy property, later the cause of internal quarrels.
updates.publicwork: Gandhi concludes that public institutions should live 'like nature, from day to day' on annual subscriptions, not permanent funds.
updates.racism: New immigration and trade laws aimed at Indians are passed in race-neutral language.
updates.indians_sa: The community's prestige rises, but so does white hostility.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is settled again in Durban with his family after the lynching, and must decide how to educate the children.
chapters.summary: Indian children are barred from white schools except by special favour, and Gandhi dislikes the mission schools. He hires an English governess and teaches the boys himself in Gujarati, keeping them at home because he believes children should not be separated from their parents. He looks ahead to his sons' later complaints about their lack of formal schooling, and to his eldest son's break with him, which he blames on his own early indulgent years. He chooses liberty over learning.

updates.gandhi: Educates his children at home rather than accept special favours. Defends the choice while admitting his sons resent it.
updates.harilal: About nine on arrival. Gandhi foreshadows that he will later break away, go to India for high school, and regard his father's later life as 'delusion'.
updates.manilal: About five on arrival in 1897; educated at home.
updates.gokuldas: About ten on arrival. Gandhi notes ahead that he will die young after a brief illness.
updates.education: Home education in the mother tongue, with liberty and self-respect valued above degrees. Gandhi links this to his 1920 call for students to leave government schools.

chapters.situation: Gandhi's law practice is thriving in Durban, but he longs for a more concrete form of service.
chapters.summary: Gandhi takes in a leper and dresses his wounds. He then volunteers two hours every morning as a dispenser at Dr. Booth's small charitable hospital, funded by Rustomji, mostly serving indentured labourers. He studies midwifery and baby care to raise the two sons born in South Africa, and delivers the last baby himself when labour comes suddenly. He argues that sex should be only for children, not lust.

updates.gandhi: Works as a hospital compounder each morning and nurses his own babies. Delivers his youngest son himself.
updates.booth: Head of St. Aidan's Mission; runs a free hospital where Gandhi dispenses medicines.
updates.rustomji: His charity funds the small hospital.
updates.khan: Covers Gandhi's magistrate's-court cases so he can serve at the hospital.
updates.kasturba: Gives birth to two more sons in South Africa; Gandhi assists at both births and delivers the last himself.
updates.ramdas: Born in South Africa (1897) and nursed by his father.
updates.devdas: Born in South Africa (1900); his father delivered him when labour came suddenly.
updates.nursing: Gandhi serves as a hospital dispenser and studies childbirth and infant care.
updates.brahmacharya: Gandhi argues that sexual union should be only for having children.

chapters.situation: Gandhi, now the father of four, is turning toward greater self-control in family and personal life.
chapters.summary: Raychandbhai asks whether a wife's devotion is truly nobler than a servant's, which leads Gandhi to rethink marriage. He tries twice to practise brahmacharya, mainly to avoid having more children, and fails. Looking ahead to 1906, he describes how leading an ambulance corps in the Zulu 'Rebellion' convinces him that public service rules out family desires. He concludes that vows open the door to freedom.

updates.gandhi: Struggles toward celibacy from about 1901, failing twice. The 1906 Zulu campaign brings him to a final resolve.
updates.raychand: His question about Mrs. Gladstone's devotion makes Gandhi rethink conjugal love.
updates.kasturba: Gandhi admits she was 'never the temptress'; the obstacle was his own will.
updates.hills: His advocacy of self-control over contraception had a lasting effect on Gandhi.
updates.allinson: His birth-control ideas had only a passing effect on Gandhi.
updates.brahmacharya: Early attempts fail because the motive is merely to avoid children. The final vow comes in 1906.
updates.vows: 'A vow, far from closing the door to real freedom, opens it.'

chapters.situation: Gandhi has been struggling toward celibacy, and the Zulu campaign of 1906 has pushed him to a decision.
chapters.summary: Gandhi takes the brahmacharya vow at Phoenix in 1906, consulting Kasturbai, who has no objection, and finds a freedom and joy he had never known. Satyagraha begins about a month later, and he sees the vow as unwitting preparation for it. He discusses control of the palate, a fruit-and-nut diet, the problem of milk, and fasting. Brahmacharya means control in thought, word and deed, which he later learns is impossible without God's grace.

updates.gandhi: Takes the brahmacharya vow in 1906 at age 36 and still finds it 'like walking on the sword's edge' at 56.
updates.kasturba: Consulted at the time of the vow; she has no objection.
updates.brahmacharya: The 1906 vow brings 'freedom and joy'. It requires control of palate, fasting and vigilance of mind, and finally God's grace.
updates.diet: Diet becomes a tool of self-restraint: limited, spiceless, ideally uncooked. Gandhi finds milk makes the vow harder.
updates.vows: Once taken, the vow becomes 'a sure shield against temptation'.

chapters.situation: Back in Durban after the lynching, Gandhi has set up a comfortable barrister's household but soon tires of it.
chapters.summary: To cut costs and dependence, Gandhi learns to wash and starch his own collars, to fellow barristers' amusement, and later irons Gokhale's treasured scarf to Gokhale's satisfaction. When a white barber in Pretoria refuses to cut his hair, he cuts it himself. He accepts the snub as punishment for Indians' own refusal to serve untouchables.

updates.gandhi: Washes his own collars and cuts his own hair, laughing off ridicule.
updates.kasturba: Gandhi teaches her the art of washing.
updates.gokhale: Looking ahead to his South Africa visit, Gandhi irons the scarf Ranade gave him for a banquet.
updates.ranade: His scarf, a gift to Gokhale, is treasured as a memento.
updates.simplicity: Self-help: Gandhi does his own laundry and haircutting.
updates.untouchability: Gandhi sees the barber's refusal as just punishment, since Indian barriers refuse untouchables.
updates.racism: A white barber in Pretoria refuses to cut Gandhi's hair.

chapters.situation: The Boer War has broken out between Britain and the Boer republics. Gandhi personally sympathizes with the Boers.
chapters.summary: Believing that rights as British citizens require Indians to help defend the Empire, Gandhi raises an Indian ambulance corps of 1,100, mostly indentured labourers, trained by Dr. Booth. After the defeat at Spion Kop they carry wounded within the firing line, marching 20 to 25 miles a day, and bear the body of Lord Roberts's son. General Buller praises them, the leaders get War Medals, and relations with British soldiers are warm.

updates.gandhi: Leads an 1,100-strong Indian ambulance corps under fire at Spion Kop; awarded the War Medal.
updates.booth: Trains and serves with the ambulance corps.
updates.buller: Asks the corps to work within the firing line and praises it in his despatch.
updates.boerwar: An Indian corps of about 300 free and 800 indentured men serves for six weeks, carrying wounded, including General Woodgate, 20 to 25 miles a day.
updates.loyalty: Gandhi's loyalty overrides his sympathy for the Boers: if Indians claim British rights, they must share British duties.
updates.indians_sa: Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Tamils and Gujaratis come to feel 'all Indians'.
updates.nursing: Gandhi's hospital experience pays off on the battlefield.

chapters.situation: The Boer War service has raised Indian prestige, and Gandhi turns to the community's own shortcomings.
chapters.summary: When plague threatens Durban, Gandhi organizes house-to-house sanitation inspections with city approval. He meets insults and indifference, and learns that it is harder to get people to do their duty than to claim their rights. The community gradually improves and the authorities' respect for him grows. Natal's Indians, even indentured labourers, contribute generously to Indian famine relief in 1897 and 1899.

updates.gandhi: Pushes self-purification as hard as rights. Learns that reform needs 'infinite patience'.
updates.sanitation: Durban house-to-house inspections. Indians are more reluctant to clean up than to claim rights.
updates.famine: Natal Indians, even indentured labourers, give generously in 1897 and 1899; the practice continues afterwards.
updates.indians_sa: The community learns, slowly, to keep homes and surroundings clean.
updates.truth: 'Truth is like a vast tree, which yields more and more fruit, the more you nurture it.'

chapters.situation: Back from war service, Gandhi fears his life in South Africa may become mere money-making and feels called to India.
chapters.summary: The community lets Gandhi go on condition that he return within a year if needed. At farewell meetings he is showered with gold, silver and diamonds, including a gold necklace for Kasturbai. After a sleepless night he puts all the gifts of 1896 and 1901 into a trust for the community. His sons agree, but Kasturbai protests in tears that the jewels are for future daughters-in-law and that she has earned them by her own service. Gandhi extracts her consent and later says a public worker should accept no costly gifts.

updates.gandhi: Leaves for India in 1901, promising to return if called. Gives all public gifts to a community trust.
updates.kasturba: Fights hard to keep the gifts, especially her necklace, arguing that her own toil counts as service. Gives in only reluctantly, and later sees the wisdom of it.
updates.harilal: Gladly agrees to return the gifts.
updates.manilal: Gladly agrees to return the gifts.
updates.rustomji: Appointed a trustee of the gifts fund.
updates.khan: Left to carry on the work in South Africa.
updates.naazar: Left to carry on the work in South Africa.
updates.gifts: All gifts from 1896 and 1901 go into a trust for the community, which still exists and grows. A public worker should accept no costly gifts.
updates.simplicity: The family is training for 'a life of service' with no costly ornaments.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is sailing home with his family, having promised Natal's Indians to return within a year if they need him.
chapters.summary: After a stop in Mauritius, Gandhi attends his first Indian National Congress, at Calcutta in 1901. Pherozeshah Mehta tells him on the train that nothing can be done for Indians abroad while Indians have no power at home, but will let him move his resolution. Gandhi stays near Tilak and watches his daily gatherings. He is dismayed by disorganized volunteers, untouchability among the delegates, and filthy latrines, which he cleans himself when no one else will.

updates.gandhi: Attends his first Congress at Calcutta and cleans latrines himself when volunteers say it is 'the scavenger's work'.
updates.pherozeshah: Tells Gandhi nothing can be done for Indians in the colonies until India has power at home, but allows his resolution.
updates.wacha: Presides over the 1901 Congress; offers to look over Gandhi's resolution.
updates.setalvad: Agrees with Pherozeshah's pessimism about helping Indians abroad.
updates.tilak: Holds court on his bed, with Motilal Ghose among his visitors.
updates.incongress: Gandhi's first session: a three-day annual show with untrained volunteers and delegates who give orders but do nothing.
updates.untouchability: Tamil delegates need a walled-off kitchen because even being seen while eating is 'pollution'.
updates.sanitation: The Congress camp is filthy, and Gandhi cleans the latrines himself.
updates.mauritius: Gandhi stays a night as the Governor's guest.

status.gandhi: In India, at the 1901 Calcutta Congress
